correspondence.finding: The northwestern modeled mainstem descends southward through the glaciated western headwater setting and the elongated northern-arm setting of Lago Argentino, then bends southeast toward the lake's central body. The federal map depicts the matching western lake geometry. APN's successfully read leaflet text separately identifies glaciers, northern lake arms and Lago Argentino in this area. This supports headwater/lake scope but does not establish a continuous river named Santa Cruz from the modeled start or identify an exact glacier-origin vertex.

The nearly straight eastward modeled passages cross the broad main body of Lago Argentino toward its eastern outlet region north of El Calafate. The federal map labels the lake and begins the eastward Santa Cruz river corridor beyond it. These display connectors and their shared junctions are lake/outlet-network structure, not evidence that the open-water passages are themselves uniformly named Río Santa Cruz.

The southwestern contribution occupies the Frías glacial/lake setting and turns north through the southern and southwestern Lago Argentino arm setting before reaching the main lake connection. The map separately shows Lago Frías, Lago Roca and the branching southwestern lake waters, while APN's text distinguishes Brazo Sur, Brazo Rico and Canal de los Témpanos. The contribution belongs to the same lake-drainage system; no single tributary name or exact arm-transition vertex is assigned to both fragments.

The northern contribution descends from the Lago del Desierto/El Chaltén setting into Lago Viedma, crosses toward its eastern outlet and then follows the southward La Leona corridor to the northeastern Lago Argentino/outlet setting. The map directly labels Lago Viedma and R. La Leona and shows their relationship to Lago Argentino. These distinct lake and connecting-river identities are retained; the model's lower junction does not by itself establish the natural mouth or a hydronym boundary.

The long eastern fragment follows the river repeatedly labeled R. Santa Cruz: an east-running sinuous valley south of the Chico–Chalía drainage, followed by a northeastward lower approach to Comandante Luis Piedrabuena. The selected end lies in the lower-river/upper-estuarine setting downstream of that town and upstream of the outer Puerto Santa Cruz coastal mouth. The map depicts the separate Río Chico approach and wider estuary, so neither the Chico trunk nor the entire outer estuary and Atlantic shoreline is assigned to this selected fragment.

The southern selected piece approaches the Lac Minto setting from the south, then turns north and northeast through the branched lake corridor toward the river outflow. The CEHQ sheet identifies Minto as a separate lake within this drainage. The small headward approach is left unassigned, and Minto is not treated as an alias of the river.

Beyond the Minto setting, the selected route follows the long northeastward outlet corridor labeled Rivière aux Feuilles on the hydrological map. The separately depicted Charpentier branch to the southeast is not substituted for the actual headward route, and the neighboring rivers draining west toward Hudson Bay are outside this connected corridor.

The middle pieces continue along the same northeast-trending trunk through the mapped tributary setting: La Goudalie and Vizien approach from the northern side, while Nedlouc and Vernot occupy the southern contributing drainage. The selected route stays on the connecting Feuilles corridor rather than following these separately named branches or turning into the more southerly Mélèzes system.

After the central eastward bend, the lower piece resumes its northeastward course south and southeast of Lac Viennaux. The independent conservation sheet shows the broad Rivière aux Feuilles reach bending northeast and then east along the reserve's southern side. Its outline and placement agree with this actual part of the selected route; Lac Viennaux remains a separate off-route lake.

The terminal piece turns north and then east toward the western Lac aux Feuilles entrance, northwest of Tasiujaq. The regional map separates this river approach from Lac aux Feuilles and the wider Ungava coastal waters. The selection does not trace the whole estuarine waterbody or the full onward passage to Ungava Bay, and no exact tidal or surveyed mouth boundary is assigned.

correspondence: The complete single selected fragment was inspected from its western interior endpoint: it first runs south, then bends east, undulates northeast and southeast, and finishes with a short northeastward approach. No separately selected tributary fragment is present.

The long western and central path crosses mapped Inland Ice. Its eastern approach reaches the glacier and inner-fjord setting north of Charcot Land, in the broader Nordvestfjord region. The original graticule, ice contours and land/fjord arrangement distinguish this corridor; the exact terminal natural-feature boundary remains unassigned.

The readable geological sheet supplies ice-sheet and marginal feature classes, but does not establish the entire modeled line as a named natural surface river, subglacial river or glacier. Nearby land, fjord and ice labels are not a uniform hydronym for the complete route.

The map legend distinguishes surface elevation, ice-thickness and sub-ice bedrock contours from river channels. Historical mapping does not establish current ice-front position, present flow or connectivity along this modeled route.

correspondence.finding: The northwestern start runs southeast before joining the upper eastward trunk. On the enlarged official basin map, this is the Cañadón Botello feeder, upstream of the Pinturas junction. It is not the farther-west Fénix Grande route through Perito Moreno, nor the separate northern El Pluma branch. Exact headwater naming limits remain unassigned.

After the western junction setting, the selected route continues toward the Pinturas and then El Pluma junctions before turning southeast. The basin map distinguishes both contributing corridors. The glacier inventory independently places the Fénix and Pinturas contributions upstream of the Pluma connection, keeping those wider headwaters separate from the selected start.

The long middle section runs generally east, south of Las Heras and the Koluel Kaike–Pico Truncado corridor, with a shallow northward bend followed by a marked southeast turn. This matches the connected river labeled Río Deseado on the provincial map, rather than the coastal drainages around Caleta Olivia.

Farther east the route crosses the RN 3 corridor south of Fitz Roy/Jaramillo, turns south and then southeast, and makes a broad southern bend before returning northeast toward the coast. Both official hydrographic maps show this distinctive lower-valley sequence, separating it from the more southerly Chico and Santa Cruz systems.

The terminal approach reaches the coastal inlet at Puerto Deseado. The province map locates the town at that inlet, and the provincial government explicitly places it on the north shore of Ría Deseado. The endpoint therefore includes a ría-mouth setting; it does not establish the precise freshwater or tidal boundary.

scope_limit: MAIN_RIV groups and model mainstem roles do not establish a uniform name for every included reach, tributary or lake passage. Source observations support only the stated representative identity or hold.
publication_boundary: Own factual observations, attribution and official public URLs only; source originals, images, complete coordinates and private evidence remain omitted.
